title: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
shortTitle: Word Break: can a string be segmented into dictionary words
keyPoints: Word Break determines whether a string can be split into a sequence of valid dictionary words.
Use 1D DP where dp[i] is true if the prefix of length i can be segmented into dictionary words.
dp[0] = true (empty prefix is trivially segmentable); dp[i] is true if some dp[j] is true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word.
Put the dictionary into a HashSet for O(1) lookups per word check.
A greedy longest-word approach fails because an early wrong cut can block a valid later split.
Time is O(n^2 * L) where L is the cost of substring and lookup; space is O(n) for the DP array.

s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i] is true if some dp[j] is true and the substring from j to i is a dictionary word.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Word Break** – determine if a string can be split into a sequence of one or more dictionary words.
- **1D DP** – `dp[i]` means the prefix of length i is segmentable; `dp[0] = true` for the empty prefix.
- **Transition** – `dp[i] = true` if there exists a j < i where `dp[j]` is true and `substring(j, i)` is in the dictionary.
- **Dictionary as HashSet** – O(1) average-case lookup for each candidate word.
- **Complexity** – O(n^2 * L) time, O(n) space for the DP array.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a legacy channel sends payment instructions as one concatenated string with no separators. Rajesh's parser must verify a clean split into known command words. A position is reachable if an earlier reachable position is followed by a valid word ending here.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Word Break DP
  ═════════════

  s = "leetcode", dict = {"leet", "code"}

  dp:  [T] [F] [F] [F] [T] [F] [F] [F] [T]
        0    1   2   3   4    5   6   7   8
                          ▲                ▲
                    "leet" found      "code" found
                    dp[0]=T            dp[4]=T

  dp[4] = true  because dp[0]=true and "leet" in dict
  dp[8] = true  because dp[4]=true and "code" in dict

  Answer: dp[8] = true
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Break is a one-dimensional dynamic programming problem over string positions. Define dp[i] as whether the prefix of length i can be segmented into dictionary words. The base case dp[0] = true means the empty prefix is trivially segmentable. For each position, look back at every earlier position and check if it is a segmentable boundary followed by a dictionary word ending at the current position.

A greedy approach fails because an early wrong cut can block a valid later split. The DP remembers every reachable boundary, so it finds a valid segmentation if one exists. Putting the dictionary into a HashSet gives O(1) lookups, and limiting the inner loop to the max word length is a practical optimisation.

The follow-up Word Break II returns all possible segmentations and needs memoised backtracking because the output can be exponentially large.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, Rajesh's parser verifies that concatenated payment instructions split cleanly into known command words before the execution engine processes them.

Remember one sentence: dp[i] is true if some earlier dp[j] is true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word, giving O(n^2) segmentation checking.
